summary: Defines a way for Diameter nodes to apply the same operation to a large group of sessions at once, instead of exchanging commands for each session. This reduces signaling load in large deployments.

eli5.summary: Instead of telling a million kids one by one to sit down, you tell the whole class once.

questions: how to do bulk operations on diameter sessions
how to apply one command to many diameter sessions
subtitle: Lets Diameter peers put sessions into groups and act on a whole group with one command instead of thousands.

tldr.problem: A single Diameter node can handle over a million sessions, but base commands act on one session at a time, so changing many sessions the same way takes many thousands of exchanges.
tldr.mechanism: Nodes tag sessions with a Session-Group-Id carried in a new optional Session-Group-Info AVP, then send ordinary commands such as Re-Auth-Request with group identifiers and a Group-Response-Action AVP that says how to follow up.
tldr.outcome: Bulk operations take a single or a few command exchanges, and any node can fall back to single-session handling by ignoring the optional AVPs.

today: RFC 9390 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2023. Neither an obsoleting nor an updating RFC is recorded for it, and it builds on the Diameter base protocol in RFC 6733.

sections.title: The Bulk Operation Problem
sections.content:
A single Diameter node in a large deployment can support over a million concurrent sessions. Sometimes a node must apply the same operation to many of them. The RFC's example is a policy decision point that needs to change the authorized quality of service for all active users with the same type of subscription.

Base Diameter commands operate on one session, so that would mean many thousands of exchanges. RFC 9390 adds session groups and ways to apply commands such as re-authentication, re-authorization, termination and abort to a whole group. It does not define a new Diameter application. It defines mechanisms and AVPs that any application can use.

The design goals are minimal impact on existing applications, optional AVPs added to existing commands, fallback to single-session operation, and implicit capability discovery when no external method exists.
sections.eli5: If a teacher has to send every student a separate note, it takes all day. With a group announcement, one message reaches the whole class.

sections.title: Session Groups and Who Owns Them
sections.content:
Once sessions are added to a group, a command that acts on the group affects every member. Either the client or the server can put a session in a group, and the assignment can change mid-session, for example when a user's subscription profile changes or the session moves to a new client during a handover.

Permissions follow ownership. The node that creates a group builds its identifier and becomes the owner. Either node can add a session to the group, but only the node that assigned a session can remove it, and only the owner can delete the group. Deleting a group means each member session is then treated individually. Applications may define a more constrained permission model.

A group identifier is carried in the Session-Group-Id AVP. It must be globally unique, must begin with the identity of the owning Diameter node, and has an implementation-defined part after a ; character.
sections.eli5: Whoever starts a club owns it. Anyone can invite a kid in, but only the person who invited a kid can send that kid out, and only the owner can close the club.

sections.title: Building and Changing Groups
sections.content:
Nodes should not use group operations with a peer unless it has advertised support. Support can come from a newly defined application's Application Id, from other means, or from the Session-Group-Capability-Vector AVP. If nothing else is used, a node SHOULD add that AVP to application messages with the BASE_SESSION_GROUP_CAPABILITY flag set. A receiver caches what it learns for the lifetime of the routing table entry for that peer and Application Id.

At session start, the client adds one Session-Group-Info AVP per group to a service-specific request such as the NASREQ AA-Request. The SESSION_GROUP_ALLOCATION_ACTION flag set means assign. The server may accept or reject the grouping, for example for lack of resources, and must echo the AVPs it received. It may also add groups of its own. If grouping is rejected, the session can still proceed as a single session. A client can also leave out the group identifier to let the server choose.

To remove a session, either side clears the allocation flag. With a group identifier it leaves that group only; with no identifier it leaves all groups. A group is deleted explicitly when its owner clears the SESSION_GROUP_STATUS flag, and implicitly when its last session is removed.
sections.eli5: Before you use the class announcement system, you check the other side has it. Then you write the club name on a kid's name tag to add them, and cross it out to remove them.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Group Commands
sections.content:
To run a command on a group, the sender appends a Session-Group-Info AVP for each group, with both the allocation and status flags set, plus a single Group-Response-Action AVP. If the command requires a Session-Id, it must name one session that belongs to at least one of the groups.

The Group-Response-Action value tells the receiver how to follow up. ALL_GROUPS (1) means one message exchange for all groups, PER_GROUP (2) one exchange per group, and PER_SESSION (3) one per impacted session. A session in several of the named groups is processed only once. With values 1 or 2, answers come only after all sessions or all sessions in a group are processed, so delay-sensitive requests SHOULD NOT use them.

If the command fails for every session, a protocol error is returned, the sender falls back to single-session processing, and the groups named are deleted. If it succeeds for some sessions, the result code SHOULD be DIAMETER_LIMITED_SUCCESS and the failed sessions are listed by Session-Id in a Failed-AVP. The sender then handles those sessions singly and removes them from the groups. Either node can also fall back to single-session mode at any time by ignoring the group AVPs, and then the response must not contain any group identifier.
sections.eli5: The teacher says to the whole class: everyone in the red group stand up. She also says whether she wants one answer from the whole class, one per group, or one from each kid.

sections.title: Commands and AVPs
sections.content:
No new commands are defined. The existing Command Code Format of a command is extended with optional AVPs. The RFC's example is a group Re-Auth-Request: the RAR gets optional Session-Group-Capability-Vector, repeated Session-Group-Info and a single Group-Response-Action, and the recipient starts re-authentication for all users in the named groups.

Five AVPs are defined, codes 671 to 675. Session-Group-Info is a Grouped AVP holding a Session-Group-Control-Vector and an optional Session-Group-Id. The control vector is a 32-bit flag field with two defined flags: SESSION_GROUP_ALLOCATION_ACTION (0x00000001) and SESSION_GROUP_STATUS (0x00000010). The capability vector has one flag, BASE_SESSION_GROUP_CAPABILITY (0x00000001), and the value 0 is reserved. No new Result-Code values are defined.
sections.eli5: The old messages keep their shape. Special stickers are added to them that say which group they are about and how to answer.

sections.title: Proxies and the State Machine
sections.content:
A stateful proxy agent must act as a server toward the client and as a client toward the server, advertising grouping capabilities and keeping session states consistent. If the proxy uses groups with the server while the client does not know about them, it must present individual session operations to the client.

A stateless proxy keeps no session state, so groups are transparent to it. The group AVPs are optional and are ignored by it and should not be removed. If one removes them anyway, the endpoints notice and fall back to single-session processing.

Appendix A gives an example of extending the authorization session state machine of RFC 6733 with group commands, written with a leading G (GRAR, GASR, GSTR and so on) for group versions of the Re-Auth, Abort-Session and Session-Termination commands.
sections.eli5: A messenger who remembers things passes the group news along carefully. A messenger who remembers nothing just carries the note without opening it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The group AVPs, including the control vector and the group id, are to be treated as security-sensitive in the same way as the Session-Id AVP in RFC 6733. Group management relies on the existing trust between client and server.

The main new risk is that a compromised client or server could launch a denial-of-service attack by terminating or changing a large number of sessions with a few commands. Diameter's transport protections cover adjacent peers only. Without end-to-end security, a Diameter agent in the path could modify the group information, and the RFC does not assume end-to-end security will be available. A proxy acting for a client or server must meet the same requirements as that client or server.
sections.eli5: A power that lets you tell a whole class what to do is dangerous in the wrong hands, so it has to stay with someone you trust.

items.label: ALL_GROUPS
items.desc: A single message exchange for all impacted groups.

items.label: PER_GROUP
items.desc: A separate message exchange for each impacted group.

items.label: PER_SESSION
items.desc: A separate message exchange for each impacted session.

items.label: Session-Group-Info
items.desc: Grouped; carries the control vector and an optional group id.

items.label: Session-Group-Control-Vector
items.desc: Unsigned32 flags for assignment and group status.

items.label: Group-Response-Action
items.desc: Unsigned32; how to follow up a group command.
